Chapter 1 — What is essence?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00074

Each thing around us has an essence—what it is—and an existence—the fact that it is. Essence is what answers the question “What is it?”, just as quantity answers “How much is it?” Under this definition, essence is a universal concept; it cannot name something known only through direct observation. It is also defined as “that by which a thing is what it is,” a wording that covers every case. This is a difference in wording, not a circular definition.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00075

Consider essence simply as essence: that is, as what a thing is in itself. It is neither one nor many, universal nor particular. Human nature, for example, exists as a particular in the world and is understood as universal in the mind. This shows that being universal or particular is not part of what humanity is in itself. Although humanity is never found without unity or multiplicity, universality or particularity, it does not follow that it must be one or many, universal or particular simply because it is humanity. The same is true of other pairs of opposites that are neither the thing itself nor part of its nature. Denying that a feature belongs to something in one respect does not rule out its belonging to it in another. And the opposite of a thing requiring one feature is simply its not requiring that feature; it does not follow that it requires the opposite.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00076

Likewise, if a possible thing has no existence at the level where we consider its essence, it does not follow that it has nonexistence there just because nonexistence is the opposite of existence. A thing can lack both opposites at one level of reality. It is only impossible for it to lack both in reality as a whole, because reality is wider than any single level. Consider things with no essential connection to one another: the existence or nonexistence of one does not occur at the level of the other’s existence or nonexistence. More precisely, when we deny a thing’s existence at a certain level, we mean that the thing is absent from that level; we do not mean that the denial itself exists there.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00077

For this reason, they say that if we are asked to choose between contradictories, the right answer is to put the denial before the respect in which we are speaking. So if we ask whether a human being, considered simply as a human being, is existent or nonexistent, the answer is: considered in itself, a human being is neither existent nor nonexistent, nor any other feature that comes to it from outside its nature. This means that none of these features is identical with humanity or part of it, even though in reality a thing is never without some of them or their opposites.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00078

Putting the denial first does not mean that the feature is not required by the essence, as some have mistakenly thought. Nor is the purpose to avoid an affirmative statement that uses a negative term, such as “not-A.” The difference between that form and a plain negative lies only in where the linking word “is” appears. If we are asked to choose between two descriptions that are treated as opposites—“a human being is one or many,” or “A or not-A”—we do not have to choose either. If we answer, we can say that, considered in itself, a human being is neither one nor many, neither A nor not-A. This differs from asking through a true pair of contradictories: there, we answer by applying the denial to each description under the stated qualification, as above. But being described by a feature does not mean that a thing is identical with that feature.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00079

Universal humanity is not one numerically single humanity shared by many people, as we have explained. Something that is one in number cannot exist in many places at once. If all people had one and the same humanity, it would have to be knowledgeable and ignorant, white and black, moving and still, and many other pairs of opposites. The relation between a universal nature and its individual cases is not like one father with many children, but like many fathers with many children. A concept that is universal in the mind can be found in each person, but no one is human merely by being related to one separate humanity set apart from everyone. Each person has a humanity of their own, numerically distinct from everyone else’s. The shared concept exists only in the mind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00080
Chapter 2 — Universals and particulars
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00081

In philosophy, a universal is something that can be shared by many individuals, or at least does not rule out being shared. A universal cannot exist as such among things in the world. If it did, it would exist as one particular thing, not as an idea that could apply to many. It could no longer be shared. Someone might object that a mental image also has its own individual existence: it belongs to one mind, has no size or position, and cannot be pointed to. Every mental image would then be particular, because an image in one person’s mind cannot be the very same image in many minds.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00082
But if a mental image is universal because it matches many things, then particulars also match one another, and would have to count as universal too.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00083

The answer is that a mental image is universal because it can match many things, not because its individual existence in one mind is shared. It exists as an idea, not as a separate thing with existence of its own. Its existence is like a shadow’s: it depends on what it is connected to, whether that thing is in the mind or outside it, and whether it comes before or after that thing. Some universals come before the many particular things they refer to, as when a cause first conceives its effects. These are called universals before multiplicity. Others are drawn from the world after particular things exist, as our general knowledge is drawn from individual things outside the mind. These are called universals after multiplicity.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00084

Here is what it means for a mental image to match many things. When you see one human being, the mind forms an image of humanity stripped of individual features. When you see another person, the mind does not need to form a second image unless the first has left your mind. It is like wax taking the impression of a seal: similar seals can be pressed against it, but they do not leave a different image each time.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00085

When books say that a universal exists in the world or can be pointed to, they mean the nature that becomes universal when it exists in the mind. Things that share a universal idea can differ in four ways. If they share only an accidental feature, they differ in what they are, as blackness and a surface do. If they share a general kind, they can differ by the feature that marks out one kind within it. If they share a specific kind, they can differ through a feature that is not required of the whole kind: anything required of the kind belongs to all its individuals, though a feature may still be required of one individual. Finally, they can differ in how fully or incompletely the shared nature is present, as we have explained before, despite the weakness of the later philosophers’ rule that a complete and an incomplete instance must differ in what they are.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00086

The truth is that a thing’s being an individual—its being impossible to share in thought—depends on something beyond its essence that prevents us from thinking of it as shared. But the feature that truly makes a thing an individual is its own existence, as the Second Teacher, al-Fārābī, held. Every existence is an individual in itself. If we set aside a thing’s particular way of existing, the mind can consider it as shareable, even if we add a thousand other features to it. Distinction in the world is not the same as being an individual in itself: distinction compares a thing with others that share something in common, while individuality concerns the thing on its own. A thing would still be an individual even if there were nothing else like it. Distinction may prepare a thing to become an individual: a material kind spread across many possible individuals does not receive existence from the highest source until its matter is ready for one of them.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00087

Some philosophers say that we know an individual through the senses or through direct awareness. This can be understood in line with what we have said: each particular existence can be known only by directly encountering it. The Illuminationist Shaykh says in al-Muṭāraḥāt that what prevents sharing is a thing’s concrete identity. But sharing is really a matter of matching, and not every kind of match counts. It must be a match with something that has no independent individual reality. A concrete identity, in the end, is the thing’s own particular existence. Yet this same Shaykh strongly insists that existence is only a mental idea and has no reality in the world. That leaves a problem: if something other than existence makes a thing an individual, it must be either the shared essence itself or that essence together with matter and other features. None of these prevents sharing; even all general ideas taken together would still be general. What, then, is this concrete identity that prevents a thing from being shared?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00088

Another view is that an individual is made particular by one of its parts, understood by analysis. This can be explained in terms of existence, since existence and essence are not separate things in the world. The claim that a maker makes something an individual is also right: a maker gives it existence, and existence is what makes it an individual. Every existence depends on its maker, so every individual depends on the maker of its existence. But we are discussing what directly makes an already existing thing an individual.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00089

Some scholars say that an individual is particular because it is connected to True Existence, the source of all things. Essences are connected to the true Maker through their existence, not through the ideas we form of them. By existing, each thing is connected to its cause, and through that cause to the cause of everything. In truth, all existences are shadows and rays of God.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00090

Others say that an individual prevents sharing simply by being what it is—not because of its parts, something necessary to it, or some feature that can come and go. The parts of a thing do not prevent sharing by themselves; something necessary to it is shared with others of the same kind; and a separable feature does not prevent sharing either. They therefore conclude that matter must be what makes an individual particular.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00091

This argument is really about what distinguishes one thing from another, which is a condition for treating it as an individual. Matter’s role in making a thing particular is like that of other features. A kind with many individuals does not come into existence as one individual until its matter is set in a particular position and time. But matter alone does not distinguish one individual from another: the same forms and shapes can occur in the same matter at different times, and then time makes the difference.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00092

The same is true of Bahmanyār’s view that individuality comes from the conditions of matter, such as position and place, when time is the same. What he means is the feature that separates two things, not what makes a nature particular in the first place. When he saw that a thing’s position could change while the individual remained the same, he said that the individualizing feature was one of the positions the thing had during its life. Unless he meant that position is a sign of an individual and something that comes with its existence, this claim would make no sense. A material individual such as Zayd cannot be thought of as shareable without considering its position.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00093

The claim that two things can help distinguish one another does not create a circular argument. To distinguish a bird from a creature that gives birth to live young, we may refer to each in terms of the other, but the knowledge of each depends on what the other is, not on first identifying the feature that distinguishes it. The distinction depends on the things themselves, or on the cause that connects them. As we will see when discussing things defined through their relations to one another, no problem follows.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00094
Objection and reply
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00095

Someone objects: if two things of the same kind differ while they share the same subject and time, then how do the parts of time differ? Time is the measure of the heavens’ motion, and that motion has one body as its subject. The parts of time should therefore have the same subject too.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00096

The answer is that the parts of time differ through their own nature. Time is a reality that is always passing and renewing; it has no nature apart from this ongoing change. Asking why one day comes before another, or how one differs from another when they are alike, is like asking why the heavenly sphere is a sphere. One day is what it is by coming before another day and differing from it. In the same way, two comes before three by nature and differs from it simply by being two.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00097

A one-cubit length of line differs from half a cubit of that line by its own nature, not because of some feature outside it. The two lengths remain different even if we set aside the place and time in which they exist. We have therefore seen that things of the same kind can differ through their own nature. Avicenna says that among the categories, only position makes something an individual by itself. He means that position distinguishes one thing from another when time is the same. With the position held the same, time can make the difference; with time held the same, position can. One position differs from another in the same way that one time or one amount differs from another: through its own nature. Individuality in this broader sense can come from a thing’s own essence, as with the Necessary Being; from something that belongs to its essence, as a position belongs to the sun; or from a feature that comes with it from the start of its existence, as with position and time. A soul is an individual through its relation to a body, and bodily powers are individuals through the bodies they belong to.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00098
Chapter 3 — Kinds of distinction
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00099

As we have seen, a thing’s being distinct is not the same as its being an individual. Being distinct is relative: it means standing apart from something else. Being an individual is not relative; it is simply the thing’s own way of existing and its identity. A distinction is what sets one thing apart from others by a feature they do not share. Sometimes that feature is the thing’s own nature, as with the Necessary Being, who is distinct from everything else simply by being Himself. Possible essences and ideas in the mind are also distinct simply by what they are. In other cases, a thing is set apart by an added feature that it has and others lack, as writing sets a writer apart from someone who does not write. Or it is set apart by lacking a feature, as not writing sets a non-writer apart from a writer.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00100

We can consider an added feature on its own, without also considering the absence of some other feature. For example, we can consider Zayd’s writing without considering that he is not a tailor. Or we can consider the feature together with the absence of another one. So an added distinction can be positive, negative, or a combination of both.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00101

A single kind of thing can be distinguished in all these ways. A human being differs by nature from a horse. One person may differ from another through a positive quality, as the merciful Zayd differs from the all-conquering Amr; or through the presence of a quality in one and its absence in the other, as a knowledgeable person differs from an ignorant one. A writer who is not a tailor differs from a tailor who is not a writer by having one feature and lacking the other; the reverse is also true.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00102

All added distinctions follow from existence. Even different kinds of nonexistence are distinct only because the ideas of them exist in our minds, or because the positive features whose absence they describe exist. Nonexistences do not have separate natures or qualities of their own. The truth is that when added qualities set things apart, it is those qualities that are truly distinct. Each is distinct in its own right, not through some further quality; otherwise, the explanation would go on without end. A thing is distinct in itself only when its difference comes from what it is, not from some added feature. When an added feature marks it out, the distinction belongs to that feature; the thing is distinct only in a secondary sense.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00103
Chapter 4 — How a general kind differs from matter, and a specific kind from its subject
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00104

How we consider a thing’s nature matters here. We can take it on the condition that it stands alone, with nothing else included. Anything joined to it is then outside it. If it forms a whole with something else, it is a part of that whole and serves as its material part. It comes before the whole both in thought and in the world, so the part cannot be treated as the whole: the two do not exist in the same way.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00105

We can also consider a thing’s nature without deciding whether it stands alone or is joined to something else. Taken this way, it can be said both of itself and of the whole it forms with the added part. A nature considered in this way may be incomplete in reality. It can apply to things with different natures, but becomes one of them only when something is added to it. This is what a general kind is: the added feature completes it and makes it one kind rather than another. A nature may instead be complete in itself, yet still take on one of several distinct forms when other features are added. Each addition makes it one of the real kinds that fall under a general kind. A specific kind is like this. The most basic matter underlying the world of elements provides an example: in itself, it is a kind, perhaps even a single individual of that kind. This has led to debate over whether its unity is the unity of a kind or of one individual. There is no real conflict: by its nature, it is a kind with only one instance.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00106

Take “animal” as an example. If we consider animal on the condition that nothing else is included, then add rationality, the whole is made of animal and rationality. Animal is the material part; it is not the whole. If we consider animal together with rationality and completed by it, we have the specific kind “human being.” If we consider animal without deciding whether anything else is included, we have a general kind. The first sense of animal is a part of a human being and comes before it in existence; the second is the human being itself; the third is its general kind. It can be said of the human being, rather than being one of its parts.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00107

We call the general kind and the feature that distinguishes a specific kind “parts” because both appear in its definition. The mind has to consider them to form an accurate idea of a specific kind that falls under a general one. In thought, this makes them prior to the specific kind. In the world, they come after it: until a human being exists outside the mind, we cannot identify a nature shared with other beings or a feature that marks it out and makes it what it is. This is the substance of Avicenna’s account in The Healing.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00108

Some questions arise about this account. First, the nature being divided is the unrestricted nature, which seems to be just the nature taken without condition. So it appears to be divided into itself and something else.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00109

The answer is that although the mind starts with the unrestricted nature, it does not consider it as unrestricted while making the division. It considers it in three ways: as the unrestricted nature itself, and as that nature taken under two other conditions. For example, the broad nature of animal is wider than “animal considered by itself” or “animal taken together with another feature.”
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00110

Second, if we take something on the condition that it stands alone, that means nothing else at all can be joined to it. How, then, can it be a part of a whole that includes something more? Avicenna uses body as an example: if we take it as a substance with length, width, and depth, and include nothing else in its nature, then sensation and growth would be outside it. Body would be matter for a whole that has those features.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00111

The answer is that “standing alone” means complete in its own nature. It does not need anything else to become what it is. If something is added, the combination is a new whole. This is different from a general kind taken without condition: that kind is incomplete and needs a feature to make it a specific kind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00112
Third, the account first treats the general kind as something taken without condition, then later describes it as taken with a condition.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00113

The answer is that “without condition” is broader. The same nature can be taken without condition in one respect and with a condition in another. What counts as a division in one respect can be the broader category in another.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00114

Fourth, a specific kind is the whole formed by the general kind and the feature that distinguishes it. So it is loose to describe it as the nature made complete by an added feature. Body, for example, does not become a human animal simply by adding a soul, sensation, and movement; the whole must be considered together.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00115

The answer is that this objection treats the general kind, the distinguishing feature, and the specific kind as different things in the world. The point is that they are one nature considered in different ways. When we consider how the general kind differs from the feature that completes it, each can be named as part of the definition and said of the whole. When we consider only their unity, we have the specific kind itself. This is what it means to take the nature “with a condition.”
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00116
Fifth, if matter is a part that exists outside the mind, why must it come before the whole in thought?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00117

The answer is that to understand a composite kind such as a human being, we must first understand its general kind and its distinguishing feature. The mind therefore considers its parts before it considers the whole. Put another way, the general kind is vague in relation to the specific features that complete it; in itself, however, it is already a distinct kind of nature. Seen in this way, it again serves as matter and as a part.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00118
Sixth, the body of an animal in the world is the body we see. How, then, can that body, taken as matter, exist before the animal?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00119

The answer is that “body” is used in two ways. The body that serves as matter for the soul is one thing; the body we call an animal is the whole formed when soul is joined to it. These are two distinct bodies, one part of the other, as in every natural compound.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00120
Seventh, a general kind can be one of its specific kinds, and a specific kind can be one of its individuals. Why, then, is the general kind called incomplete and the specific kind complete?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00121

The answer is that we are considering kinds as the mind understands them, not as they exist outside the mind or as the senses point to them. The general kind is incomplete because it needs a feature to make it a complete kind. The specific kind is complete: it does not need a further feature to become what it is. This does not mean that actual individuals lack features that distinguish them from one another.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00122

Keeping this difference in mind, we can take a distinguishing feature in three ways. If we take it on the condition that nothing else is included, it is a part and a form. If we take it without deciding whether it is joined to something else, it can be said of the whole and is still a distinguishing feature. If we take it together with what it completes, it is the specific kind itself. We can consider an accidental feature in the same three ways: as the feature, as something said of a thing, or as the whole made from the feature and the thing it belongs to. The first whole has a real unity in its nature; the second is one only in the way we consider it.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00123

It would be clearer to call a specific kind, when considered as the thing that bears features, a “subject” rather than “matter.” The same applies to a general kind considered in relation to accidental features, rather than to features that complete its nature. Matter needs what is joined to it in order to become a complete thing; a subject already exists without the feature that belongs to it. The same thing can be matter for one feature and a subject for another.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00124

Here is a point to note. A general kind is incomplete and needs a distinguishing feature as part of what it is. It cannot need that feature in one case but not another. If it became complete without the feature, it would no longer be a general kind. A simple nature therefore cannot lose its distinguishing feature and have another one take its place. The feature is not needed just to set the thing apart from others, since accidental features can do that too. It is needed because the nature itself is incomplete. A kind cannot depend on a distinguishing feature in one case and not another, except as a difference in how the mind considers it.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00125

There is also a difference between a general kind in a compound thing and a general kind in something simple. In a compound, a general kind can be considered apart from its role as a general kind and taken as a complete kind in its own right, without adding one particular distinguishing feature. For example, body is a substance with length, width, and depth. Its nature is complete; otherwise, body could not change from something lifeless into a plant or an animal. Body is a general kind only when we consider it without deciding whether anything else is included. Taken this way, “body” applies to animals, plants, and other bodily kinds: they are all substances with three dimensions, even though they are more than just that.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00126

But a simple kind such as color cannot have a separate existence outside the specific forms that give it its character. There is no color in the world alongside black or white that combines with them to make each color, as body exists alongside a living form to make an animal. What is reported—that making the general kind and the distinguishing feature is one act, so making body is the same as making animal—if it is correct, means that making body as a general kind is not separate from making a specific kind. Considered in itself, however, the general nature exists in a different way from the feature that distinguishes the specific kind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00127

It is also wrong to say that when an animal dies, its body disappears and a different body begins. Some matter must remain to receive the changing forms and features, whether it is a simple body or prime matter. That underlying matter is the most general material part of compound things. The animal’s bodily nature remains after death, though it is no longer an animal’s body. To say that its identity has been destroyed and replaced by another comes close to the wild claims that things can leap from one place to another without passing through the space between, that parts can separate and remain, or that qualities cannot last.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00128

One further point: you may read that if a general nature must be made one particular kind, it cannot exist as another; if it does not have to be made that kind, its joining with it may be by chance. This only makes sense when the general nature has a form in the world. It does not work for color in relation to black and white. Color itself has no form in the world separate from the power by which sight distinguishes colors. We cannot point to color apart from its forms and ask why it became black or white. But body and prime matter do exist in the world. If body had to take one particular form in order to exist, there could be no body without that form. So there must be a cause beyond body itself that makes it fire, a heavenly body, moving, located, round, or otherwise. This leaves room for matter to remain while forms and other features change.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features

Chapter 5 — How to identify a kind’s distinguishing feature, how it differs from a mere mark, and how it joins the general kind
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00130

The words used for a kind’s distinguishing feature in definitions often name signs of the true feature, or things that follow from it. “Sensitive” and “moving,” for example, are not, by their meanings alone, the features that define an animal. The true feature is that it has a soul that perceives and moves. The ability to perceive and the ability to move are not the animal soul itself; they are among the things that follow from it. But because we may not know the true features, or may lack names for them, we sometimes have to use these signs instead. So “sensitive” does not mean the concept formed from a feeling or a relation of awareness. Otherwise, one thing would be made up of things from different categories, though one thing belongs to two categories only by accident. The true distinguishing feature is what gives rise to these qualities, and the same applies in similar cases. When one meaning is considered together with another, if they differ in what they are and how they exist, the second is not a distinguishing feature but a quality added from outside. If they differ only because one is vague and the other makes it specific, then the second is a distinguishing feature. Avicenna says in the metaphysics section of The Healing: “The mind may grasp a meaning that could be many things, each of which is that same meaning in existence. It then adds another meaning to make it specific, by including it in the first. This second meaning differs only in how definite or vague it is, not in its existence.”

Further discussion and clarification
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00132

Some have denied that simple things have parts that the mind can distinguish. They say these parts are only features that go with the thing: the feature shared by several things is their general kind, and the feature unique to one is what distinguishes it. But this would mean that simple things with entirely different natures share an added quality, without anything in common to explain why it belongs to them. To avoid saying that one meaning can be drawn from different natures, these thinkers claimed that both the general kind and its distinguishing feature in a simple nature come from qualities that belong to it in the world. The broader kind is drawn from a feature we are not sure belongs only to that nature. The feature that distinguishes it, by contrast, is drawn from one we know belongs to that nature alone. This view is plainly strained.

What led them to it was the thought that blackness, for example, could be divided into color and a quality that makes the eye contract. If both match blackness completely, there is no difference between them. But if color alone matches blackness, then it also matches whiteness, so blackness and whiteness would have to be the same thing. If only one of the two matches blackness, then blackness would be just that one. And if each matches a different part of blackness, then blackness would be made of parts in the world, though we have assumed it is simple. From this, they conclude that the general kind and distinguishing features of simple things are only ways the mind considers them. Blackness, for example, exists in the mind just as it does in the world, so it has no essential parts.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00134

Here is how the difficulty can be resolved. If every meaning we drew from a nature were a complete and distinct reality, that nature would itself be made of parts. If one complete thing is identical with a second, and the second with a third, then the first must also be identical with the third. But the meanings we draw from a nature are not all complete in that way. Some are incomplete in themselves, or the mind considers them without yet giving them a definite form. Others make them definite. Bringing these meanings together is more like bringing a capacity to fulfilment, or something incomplete to completion. It does not mean that the nature itself is made of separate parts. Similarly, a general nature may be present in different things without making them identical. Animal nature belongs to both a human being and a horse, yet a human being and a horse are different.

To understand this more clearly, notice that not all the meanings we draw from a thing are drawn in the same way. Some come from a thing as it is in the world; others come from how the mind considers it. The mind can take a meaning that is mixed and joined with definite features in reality, think of it on its own as vague and undetermined, and then add specific meanings to it. This is not like joining two complete, separate things in reality, as matter and form join to make a third thing. Rather, the two meanings differ only because one is vague and the other makes it definite. The first kind of joining creates a real compound; the second creates a compound in thought, though this way of thinking can still be true at its own level of reality.

Someone might ask: if we take both the general kind and the distinguishing feature from a simple nature, then think of them as matter and form, each seems complete in itself. Wouldn’t joining two complete things mean that the simple nature is really made of parts? After all, different things cannot match one simple nature.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00137

The answer is that the general kind and the distinguishing feature are not taken from a simple thing as two complete things, so that the general kind becomes mental matter and the distinguishing feature mental form. The mind alone makes the simple nature seem to be a compound of matter and form. There is no such compound in the thing itself. This is something the mind imagines through a way of considering the thing that does not match the world outside the mind.
Stage Four — Essence and its related features

Someone might ask: if a definition tells us what a thing is, how can the definition contain several distinct meanings when the thing itself is simple, with no parts except those the mind imagines?
Stage Four — Essence and its related features
passage-en-00139

The answer is that a definition lays out, one by one, the meanings drawn from a thing’s nature. The thing itself holds them together as one. So the definition can have several parts without the thing itself being made of parts, even when the definition and the thing are one and the same in nature. We have already seen how the mind can draw different meanings from one simple nature.
